text: Continuous-time Kelly for one risky asset with drift m, volatility s and risk-free rate r: f* = (m - r)/s^2, growth g(f) = r + f(m - r) - s^2 f^2 / 2 (an exact parabola in f), and maximum growth g(f*) = r + (m - r)^2 / (2 s^2) = r + S^2/2, where S is the Sharpe ratio. The fraction f is a multiple of equity, so f above 1 is leverage. Because f* x s = S, the Kelly-consistent annualised volatility target equals the Sharpe ratio. (high confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: Carver's translation of Kelly into a volatility target: with Gaussian returns the full-Kelly annualised risk target equals the expected Sharpe ratio (expected SR 0.5 means 50% annualised risk). He calls half Kelly 'a far safer bet', cut his own target to 25% a year ('closer to the 10 - 20% that most systematic trend following firms target'), and halves backtested performance as a rule of thumb because most backtests are overfitted. Thorp's identity f* x s = S gives the same result. (medium confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: ECB Financial Stability Review box (May 2020; the page gives only the month): a stylised four-asset risk-parity portfolio would have had to sell assets worth nearly 225% of its capital to meet its volatility target in March 2020, leaving a cash share near 25%. Estimates of money in volatility strategies run up to USD 2 trillion, including about USD 300 billion in some 100 risk-parity funds. The ECB says the model figures are not observed data and the contribution of these strategies to price moves 'remains hard to quantify'. (low confidence) (verified as of 2020-05-01)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: Fixed-fractional sizing: choose the fraction of current equity to lose if the stop is hit, then size = equity x risk% / |entry - stop|. Kraken, Tapeboard and The Right Trader give this formula. Because the base is current equity, dollar risk grows with the account and shrinks after losses. Kraken: 'A common approach is to risk 0.5% to 2% of account per trade'; The Right Trader: the fraction is 'something you choose' and 'not a forecast', and 1% is 'a common retail choice, not a law'. (high confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: De-risk as drawdown grows. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba: practitioners who wish to protect capital above all 'sharply reduce risk as their drawdown increases'. The original Turtle rules, as reproduced on a blog, cut the notional account by 20% for each 10% drawdown, so position size shrank faster than equity. (medium confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: Volatility targeting sets exposure inversely to forecast volatility, so portfolio risk stays constant rather than notional exposure: leverage up when volatility is low, down when it is high. Moreira and Muir scale monthly returns by c divided by the previous month's realized variance (inverse-variance scaling); Harvey et al. scale by sigma_target divided by a volatility estimate known 24 hours ahead (inverse-volatility scaling), which they note has lower turnover than variance scaling. (high confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional

text: Kelly sizing maximizes the expected log of wealth, which maximizes the limiting exponential growth rate of wealth. Thorp's Theorem 1: if the per-bet growth rate g(f) is above zero, wealth tends to infinity almost surely; if g(f) is below zero, wealth tends to zero almost surely (ruin is almost sure); at g(f) = 0 wealth oscillates between 0 and infinity. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba name the main drawback: the suggested wagers can be very large, so Kelly is very risky in the short term. (high confidence)
keywords: Position sizing Kelly volatility targeting fixed fractional
